utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, please proceed to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, and Skye Winner for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham, and good morning to you both. And good morning also to Mr. Ackerman who is not with us today. And I start with you, Mr. Cunningham, and Mr. Ackerman, I suppose you will convey to him our -- the Chamber's best wishes on Thanksgiving Day. So you have filed a so-called Defence first motion for protection. I consider it the second actually because there was a first one which was not exactly -- which did not exactly have the result that you were anticipating and that we were anticipating anyway. Our decision that we are communicating to you now is that -- rather, first, let's see what the Prosecution has to say about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection. So if there is no objection, I think we can proceed to accept the motion with the understanding, Mr. Cunningham, that at the beginning of the testimony of that particular witness, we will go into closed session for a while, we'll interview him to make sure the provision is necessary and indeed the one which should be put in place. Otherwise, you don't have to worry; it will be granted as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I move the books right here so I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, again, yes. Chuqing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It shouldn't be you, Mr. Cunningham. Francesca, it's not that I wouldn't like to see you, but I think for today you have to be patient. Is the witness here? Do we have any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I think the only thing and we're going to leave it until Mr. Cunningham's had a chance to talk to Ackerman. We're slightly confused now, again, I'm afraid, about what witnesses are coming next week, but I think we can leave it until the end of today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We're still set on the first two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 31 and 33 in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is one other thing I want to inform the Chamber about this next witness. He is a little bit hard of hearing, and I've told him about the procedure, but I wanted to let the Court know about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We have a problem, we'll see how we tackle it. But I think the usher puts on the volume, that should help.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There's one final matter, Your Honour. I made an exhibit book that has the relevant exhibits except for one in B/C/S. I have that available and I've had the usher pull the English exhibits. Apparently some of the DB exhibits that are on my list have already been introduced as Prosecution exhibits,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And Ms. Richterova has promised to correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes, could we bring the witness in, please. Thank you. No protective measures for this witness, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bojinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to The Hague and to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are very shortly going to start giving evidence in the trial instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin. And our Rules require that before you start testifying, you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath and that in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So you have the text of the solemn declaration in your hand. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair. I notice that you are a little bit excited, nervous. You don't need to be. I want you to feel as comfortable as possible while you give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And everyone will try to make things easy for you. You have been summoned as a Defence witness, and you will be examined first by Mr. Cunningham who I suppose -- I presume you have met already. He will ask you a number of questions, and then he will be followed by Madam Richterova, the lady -- the second starting from your right. And that will be cross-examination. You will be asked questions, and your duty under the solemn declaration that you entered is to answer each and every question as fully and as truthfully as possible, independently of who is asking you the question. In other words, you cannot and shouldn't even try to make a distinction between questions coming from the Defence and questions from the Prosecution. Everyone has a right to ask you questions here, and you have a duty to answer each question in the same manner, that is truthfully and as comprehensively as possible. I would also suggest that you keep your answers as concise as possible, and that will ensure that you will be back home before the end of the week is over. It very much depends on you. Thank you. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Milos Bojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Again, remember what His Honour has told you about listening to the question and answering only the question that is asked of you. If you look right to your left, you'll see a notebook, and that notebook has some exhibits in it. This is the exhibit book I talked about with you yesterday. It's on the table right next to you, right next to your left elbow. At the appropriate time I'll have you go to the exhibit. But we're not there yet. What I wanted to do is ask you some questions to get started. Tell us how old a man you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what municipality were you born in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where do you currently reside, what municipality? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What is your profession? What do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a teacher of the Serbian language at a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is that secondary school in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you been a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: 29 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where did you complete your secondary school studies at?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where did you attend university at?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what year did you get your diploma, your degree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: 1973, January of 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Save for your -- except for your one-year compulsory military duty, have you continuously taught since 1973?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In 1990, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in 1991, did you join a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And which party did you join?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And after you joined -- after you became a member of the SDS, were you a regular party member, or did you have a position of authority within the party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In 1990, 1991, as a party member living in Glamoc, did you ever travel to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how often would you travel to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: To the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to listen carefully. Remember, my question was how often would you travel to Banja Luka, not where did you go. But how often did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean by what means of transportation? I used my own private car. I'm not sure I understand your question. How frequently, what does the "how" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of interpretation actually probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When I say how frequently, did you go once a month, three times a year? How often would you go?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Three times a year, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in 1991 on one of those trips to Banja Luka, did you meet the defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by chance, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How is it by chance that you met him in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There's always the off chance that you meet someone in the street, that someone introduces you to someone else. And that's precisely how I met Mr. Brdjanin, although I had previously been aware of his involvement in sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember where within the city of Banja Luka that you met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At the Bosna Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And was there any political event going on within the Hotel Bosna when you met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, this would usually not take place in hotels, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. So what were the circumstances that you met him? Did someone introduce you to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As for the circumstances, we were just sitting there over a drink. There were about ten people there. Mr. Ljupko Racic was the one who introduced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the ten people who were sitting there in the Hotel Bosna, were you talking about politics?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And was there a discussion going on about politics and what should happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed politics also because the situation in that area was complex. The discussion was just an ordinary one; no particular plans were being hatched as to what could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In this conversation, in this discussion, did you let your position, your thoughts on the situation, be known?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What did you tell the ten people, including Mr. Brdjanin, who were seated talking politics?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The conversation about the complex nature of the situation was of a more general kind. I spoke about the need for every intellectual to show common sense, to try to be active in their own environments, to try to explain to those who are less knowledgeable, to try to tell them to remain calm, to not provoke incidents. The times were such, the times required calm because the times were complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you made this statement, participated in the discussion, did you have non-Serb friends and colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, just in general, back at school, back at --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Does your family have many mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how do you personally accept the fact that you have family married to non-Serbs? Is that something that bothers you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was something that was normal. It's, I dare say, a norm of civilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How long did this discussion that you've described for us, this conversation with the other men, how long did it go on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say with any degree of precision, but perhaps for about half an hour, as long as it took to drink a coffee or any other drink at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time of this discussion when Mr. Brdjanin was there, did you ever go up to him and ask him for any sort of job, any sort of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was this the first time you met Mr. Brdjanin in person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you were mobilised when the war started. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you remember the date that you were mobilised and entered the military?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what date was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The 13th of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you sure --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. When did the war begin? When did the war begin? I think it was in 1992, yes. Right. Okay. The 13th of April 1992, the mobilisation took place in my area, and I was a member of the army, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you sent to the front, or near the front?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: To the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I know this is Ms. Richterova's witness, but I want to make the point. A lot of these questions are leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usually as you know, I have taken the practice that I will not -- most of the questions are actually from both sides. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But usually I do not interfere unless there is an objection. The moment there is an objection, of course, I do interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It may be important, and I anticipate this may be important, a leading question like "were you sent to the front" is not one I think should be asked. "Where were you sent" is the proper question. In essentials, I have no objections to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On matters that may be important, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have taken it that amongst you, you accept leading questions most of the time. When you have an objection or a reservation, then just point that out. I do share Ms. Korner's objection. Perhaps you can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where were you sent to, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent to the front where -- to the border of three municipalities, Glamoc, Livno, and Kupres where the borders meet. There is the -- there is a very dominant feature there, Mount Cincar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what were your job duties, if any, when you were at this area you just described?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: A common soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to hand you Prosecution Exhibit 241.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And Mr. Bojinovic, in that grey notebook right by your left elbow, open it up, and you'll see a tab that has the number 241 on it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if you could speak up. Something's wrong with my microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the yellow tabs, attached to those documents you'll see the -- you should see the number 241. I believe it's the very first document there. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: For the record, this document is a decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff appointing you as chief of the agency for population movement and exchange of material wealth for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you receive this document while you were in military service?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Tell the Chamber the circumstances under which you received this document, how was it delivered to you, what you did with it when you got it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: While I was at the front, I was informed verbally of my appointment. I received approval by my command to report to this new duty. And when I came to Banja Luka on the 1st of July, I received this document. I got it from the secretary of the AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Was this a position that you had requested, a position that you had lobbied for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not ask for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you received notice that you had a new job assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was just a normal reaction because it is quite normal to merely do the jobs that are somehow imposed by the situation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After speaking with your commanding officers about this new assignment, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not talk to the commanders. But after having received this decision, I went to the building housing the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where was that building located, in what municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The face of Prosecutor's Exhibit 241 is dated 12 June 1992. Do you remember how soon after 12 June 1992 you reported to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was the reason for the delay of between 12 June and 1 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it took a while for the decision to arrive to the command at Glamoc. There was a war on. And since I was on the front line, away from the town, probably that was the reason. Therefore, the mail did not take its regular route as in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you arrived in Banja Luka on or about 1 July 1992, who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I said it was exactly on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if the interpreter could speak up. But let me answer your question. I met with the secretary of AR Krajina, Boro Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where did you meet with him at?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we said hello to each other, and I received this decision appointing me chief of the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagojevic give you any information, give you any instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Not much, just that the building was situated near a bridge. That was all. Near the town bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you surprised by the information or the lack of information that you got from Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And why were you surprised?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I expected someone to escort me to the agency building, but there was no one, save for Blagojevic. Probably that could have been the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagojevic give you any instructions as to what your job duties or job responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did he give you any information as to what the agency's purpose was, what function it served in the community?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that you met Mr. Blagojevic, the secretary to the ARK. During that day, did you meet anyone else from the ARK or the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After you got the location of the agency from Mr. Blagojevic, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was not familiar with Banja Luka, I spent some time looking for the building since there are many bridges in Banja Luka. It took me an hour, hour and a half to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And on 1 July 1992, was that your first day as the chief of the agency for population movement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You started work on 1 July 1992. When was your last day with the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you precisely what date it was. But the agency did operate until the end of the year. It might have stopped in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say "the end of the year," what year are you talking about, just so that's clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: From 1 July 1992 until the end of the year 1992, did you have any personal face-to-face contacts with the defendant, Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you have any telephonic contact with him during this same time period --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you receive any written documents, written instructions from Mr. Brdjanin during this same time period? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During this same time period, 1 July 1992 to the end of the year of 1992, did you have any personal contact with any other representative of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you meet with -- did you know any -- did you know about the Crisis Staff for the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Had you heard of that when you assumed this position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And -- I'm going to go ahead and change topics now. We're still on 1 July 1992, Mr. Bojinovic, but I want to have you tell the Chamber about the agency. How long did it take you to actually locate the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: An hour or an hour and a half perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where was the agency physically located?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the fort Kastel, near the bank of the Vrbas River.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, did the agency have offices?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Chamber what the offices looked like, how big they were, what sort of equipment was available?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was an older building, and only partly made operable and to be used for an office. And the rooms had very small square areas. They were maybe 4 by 5 metres, square metres. There was no luxury furniture or electronic equipment there. We had one telefax device, a telephone, logbooks, a car. It was an official car. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay, you just answered my question that I was interrupting. When you went to work there -- first of all, in that notebook, look on the tabs. You'll see a tab that has the number 290 on it. Go to that document, that tab, 290, because I want to ask you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we put it on the ELMO. And I think this is one of our exhibits. I think it's P1687.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you found that document, Mr. Bojinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When I ask you to look at a document, I want you to take as much time as you need to read the document to make sure that you're familiar with it. So let me know when you're ready because I want to ask you a question about this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is this document a payroll document for the agency for the month of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We see your name next to number one. And then underneath it we see two, three, four, five names.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you arrived there, how many employees did the agency have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The four employees present here under numbers two, three, four, and five.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who was Bandic Perka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Perka Bandic was Slobodan Bandic's wife. He also worked in the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was Ms. Bandic's duties? What were her responsibilities with the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: She performed secretarial duties and other duties, when and if necessary. But the duties of a secretary, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And Slobodan Bandic, her husband, what were his duties, his obligations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: His duties were of an operative nature, to escort passengers and provide security to them. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The fourth name is Stevo Gojanovic. What was his duties?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Being an occupational invalid, his duty was to simply register the persons applying to the agency for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what do you mean by an "occupational invalid"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: His hands were disabled. His fingers were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the very last name that we see there, what was that individual's --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Ljilja Miljkovic. She was cleaning the premises, airing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As you stayed with the agency, did you add more employees as the year went on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The persons came applying for assistance, and there was need for more labour force. We hired more people when the circumstances permitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you because I want you to go look at another exhibit. Looking at the yellow tab on the documents, go to the exhibit that is marked 277.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it is also Prosecution Exhibit P1688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Look at that document, make sure you're acquainted with it, and let me know when you're done reading it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This document, you mean 277?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It appears that there are now 11 employees. Why were the additional --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why were the additional people hired on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Because the scope of work was such that four people weren't enough to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How soon after you arrived was it necessary to get more employees?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say we hired one or two people a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We've talked about --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps even three. They weren't all employees at one time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You've told us what some of the individuals listed in Exhibit 277 did. But let's talk about the new ones. The person next to number 4, Milan Segrt, what was that individual's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Segrt was a refugee from Livno. He worked together with Slobodan Bandic. They discharged operative duties, escorting and providing security to passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The individual listed next to number 6, tell us that individual's name and what their job responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Ankica Luzaic was in charge of registering persons and providing assistance to persons who applied to the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What do you mean by "registering persons"? I may be getting ahead of myself with that question, but what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Just as Stevo Gojanovic was doing that, it actually took more than one person to do that. You had to enter the person's first and last name, and then also write down the description of what they were asking for, what kind of an assistance, and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. The individual next to number 7, tell us the name and what that individual's duties were.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Valentina Budimic, she was a lawyer by profession. And she was there employed in the agency in case citizens may appear asking for some sort of clarification regarding their documentation. But practically, Valentina didn't have much to do. She was there just in case there might be something for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What about number 8, Radovan Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: A refugee from Livno, and he did the accountancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. The next name is Mira Borkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: A typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And tell us about the person at number 10, who is that and what was that person's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: A refugee from Bugojno, also a typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived at the agency on 1 July 1992, was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. agency already in operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of why the agency was formed and what its original function was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The agency was established with the aim of assisting people of all ethnicities in the area of the AR Krajina because there was a war on. In order to prevent the population from suffering the war and to prevent any illegal acts, and unfortunately there were many of such acts present in all ethnicities, the agency was established for the purpose of protecting the people and providing them with the necessary assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you went down the list of employees, you told us that several of those employees were refugees. Were those individuals that you described as refugees --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were those individuals that you described as refugees, were those Serbs or non-Serbs? I'm just talking about the ones that worked for the agency.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just a moment, please. Valentina Budimic is married to a Croat. I don't know, however, which ethnicity she belongs to. Mira Borkovic, I don't know which ethnicity she belongs to. I know that Milan Segrt is a Serb. And Stevo Gojanovic as well, just as Radovan Jovic. As for Ankica Luzaic, I couldn't tell her ethnicity. Now, in the cases where I cannot guess the ethnicity, I think the people actually come from mixed marriages or they might be of Croat or Serbian ethnicity. But I'm not sure, nor did I really ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the agency provide -- well, let me back up. In 1992, had any Serbs come to Banja Luka as refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the agency provide any assistance to Serbian refugees in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning. At the beginning, it was only Serbs who applied for assistance because they were the ones who were refugees for the most part. Later on, as the war between Croats and Muslims broke out in the territory of the Federation, then both Muslims and Croats applied, as well as Slovenians, Hungarians. Therefore, the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived there 1 July 1992, was the agency one that was solely assisting Serbian refugees or had it changed as you had described?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, the agency assisted all the people who applied for help. Therefore, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Slovenians, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Using the notebook, I want you to go to the tab that is marked with the number 260. Let me know when you find that document and when you're done reading it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- One of your documents, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, no. Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This document is meant to be used to familiarise those citizens who apply to the agency for help with the fact that the agency may be able to perform some of these specific tasks at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let's very briefly talk about these functions. Number one talks about organising bus travel on routes from Banja Luka-Gradiska, and then in parentheses to Zagreb, and then Banja Luka-Vlasic, and then in parentheses, to Travnik. We'll cover this in more detail shortly, but did the agency actually provide these services?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Citizens would come to the agency to help them travel to Zagreb or to Travnik. The agency always found a way to be of service to those people. So yes, the answer is the agency did perform those services.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And remember not only what I've told you, but more importantly what His Honour has told you, to listen carefully to the question and answer only the question. And I'm not mad at you for this, but this could have been answered with a simple yes or no. So keep that in mind, please, as we go through this. The next thing, number two says: "The agency organises furnish removal using trucks. Truck transport is based on a three-room apartment. That is, it can transport belongings of two or three individuals who will pay for the truck together." The service of furniture removal, did the agency ever actually remove furniture for individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why was that? Why couldn't that be done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This was not possible in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The third entry under Exhibit DB260 says that a service provided by the agency is it organises a convoy of private luxury vehicles. "The car must be cancelled at the CSB, and the trial -- and the trial registration plates obtained. The technical goods that are being transported must be taxed at customs, and the customs declaration must be kept. Personal items should be listed, and the list verified at the agency." My first question with respect to that service was did the agency ever actually provide organised convoys of private luxury vehicles leaving the Municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For persons who had small children, those were not precisely luxury vehicles, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the time that you were the chief of the agency, how many vehicles actually left?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But if it's necessary, I could say up to five, six, perhaps ten vehicles a month. I can't be sure, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Look at -- go now to the tab that is marked Exhibit 254. When you locate that document, take your time reading it and let me know when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. 254.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: First of all, who is DD D-O-M-E-T, DD DOMET in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That's an agency based in Zagreb which tried to run business in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was only natural for us to get in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This document is -- and we're getting a little bit far afield, and it's my fault. But this document is entitled "a contract on cooperation." Was this contract ever finalised? Was there ever a final agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Go down to the very last entry, the entry number is number 10. That entry says: "The issue of luxury vehicles remains to be solved." During the time that you were the chief of the agency, was it ever possible to arrange a convoy of luxury vehicles to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure. I asked why was it not possible to arrange a convoy of luxury vehicles to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever had an expensive or luxury vehicle would have gone long before the agency was there to give them a hand. Secondly, in wartime, it just wasn't possible. The reaction of other people, bystanders and onlookers would have been unpredictable, those watching the cars and convoys of luxury cars leaving the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let's go back to Exhibit 260, that's the exhibit that you looked for, looked at earlier that talks about services provided by the agency, because I want to talk to you about the last two services that are listed in this document dated 25 November 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are you back to that exhibit, sir, to number 260?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Number 4 says: "The agency conducts exchange of apartments/houses and other material assets. In fact, the agency's task is to act as a middleman between the interested parties." Now, we're going to talk about this in more detail in just a minute. But yes or no, was the agency able to provide that service to people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What about number 5? Let's go back to number 4. You just told me that no, they were not able to provide that service to people. Did the agency have a function trying to assist people with apartments, with flats?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And tell us very briefly what the agency's purpose was, what they did to assist people who had flats?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: People who had flats or houses would address the agency asking the agency whenever it was possible to find them people with similar problems. The agency would then put these people in touch, and they would then proceed to sort out their own business and needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about that in just a minute. But let's finish up this document by talking about number 5, services provided by the agency. Number 5 says: "Makes a contract between the parties who manage to agree on an exchange." You told us that you had a lawyer on staff. Did this lawyer provide the contracts that are discussed in number 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was the agency ever able to provide the service listed in number 5?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This was the competence of judicial organs, not of the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to talk about the conducting of exchange of apartments and houses that's referenced in number 4. You just told us a minute ago that people who had flats or houses would address the agency asking whenever it was possible to find them people with a similar problem. Let's go into a little bit more detail now. How would that work? Let's assume I am a Croat. I have come to Banja Luka, and I have a flat -- I own a flat or have access to a flat in Zagreb. If I came to the agency, what services could you provide to me?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: You come to the agency. You say that you own a flat in Banja Luka. You want to go to Zagreb and swap your flat for the same kind of flat in Zagreb. The first thing we had do is look through our records, through our files, to see whether we had any people on file who had arrived from Zagreb offering the same kind of thing. Whenever we found such people on our lists, we would put them in touch with each other. We give them phone numbers, or they would use our offices to make phone calls, get in touch with each other, make appointments. And then they would probably reach some kind of an agreement between themselves. That's where our job stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now -- and my question made no sense because I just said I'm a Croat who has come to Banja Luka. So let's just assume that I was a Croat living in Banja Luka with a flat, and I wanted to go back to Croatia. When I showed up at the agency, what would I do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you should inform us about your problem, the problem being that you actually own property in Banja Luka and want to find an equivalent in Zagreb and are ready to travel. Then a replacement would be found for you, or some other flat that you may like. That's where our service ends as concerns your property. As for the second thing, your readiness to travel, there are several steps to be gone through. But we can discuss that once you actually ask me the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you for that. Where would the information be kept? I am the Croat who owns the flat in Banja Luka, and I want to exchange it. Would that be posted on the wall, anywhere within the office? How would that work?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Information on citizens addressing the agency was kept secret. If there was a citizen who did not wish his information to be displayed on the bulletin board, this was complied with. If the citizen wanted to make his personal information public, then this information would be placed outside the agency on a pane of glass where everyone could see it. And then they could look for people with similar problems and similar cases, and just get in touch without any assistance whatsoever from anyone in the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, did the agency charge a fee for serving as the middleperson?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, pursuant to municipal regulations. This would have been the normal fee charged for administrative services, for phone services, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you remember what that administrative fee would have been back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but it was in the regulations of the town's administration. It was all pursuant to law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would you -- I know you can't remember the specific numbers. But would you characterise it as a high administrative fee, a low administrative fee? How would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not high, not low. Just usual. If you make a cash withdrawal totalling 100 euros in a bank, the bank officials will probably charge you a fee for their service. So this is the usual thing to do. And our fee was the usual fee which was precisely stipulated in the regulations of the municipal authorities. This was not down to any personal decision taken by any individual; this was all done according to regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what would happen with the money that was collected, this administrative fee? Where would it go?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The money would go to the agency's account, the agency's account, the account that the agency had. Accurate records were kept, and money was immediately placed into the account.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was information about that account, the agency's accounts, posted openly, publicly within the office of the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only the head accountant had this information, those people who were in charge of the specific tasks. There was no need to publish this information in our offices. This kind of information is never published in any company. You don't exactly put this kind of thing on a bulletin board.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And who had control over the account? Who had signature privileges or authority over that account?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The head accountant, Mr. Radovan Jovic. He was in charge of control. He monitored the transactions, further signatories were the head of the agency, and the secretary, Perka Bandic. Whenever necessary, she was authorised to make withdrawals from the bank on behalf of the agency, and she only did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. We're at that point where I want to talk with you and to have you inform the Chamber about one of the services provided by the agency, and that is listed at number 1. It says: "Organises bus travel from Banja Luka to Gradiska, Banja Luka to Vlasic." While you were the chief of the agency, and if you need to find an exhibit, go back to Exhibit 260, while you were chief of the agency --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- did the agency, in fact, arrange travel between Banja Luka to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not Zagreb. As far as the border which was controlled by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the -- while you were chief of the agency, did the agency actually provide service from Banja Luka all the way to Travnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Not all the way. Only as far as the Muslim-controlled line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to both the Croat-controlled line and the Muslim-controlled line, what would happen at that point to individuals that were on buses leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there would be vehicles there waiting for people who were travelling to their destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Which of these two routes, Banja Luka to Gradiska or Banja Luka to Vlasic, which one of them was travelled more frequently?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the roughly six months that you were at the agency, on the average, per month, how many buses would leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three, sometimes only one. Sometimes two. It only occurred once that there were actually six buses leaving. So the main value would have been two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I think you might have misunderstood my question. I'm not talking about how many buses might have been in a convoy; I'm just talking about the frequency, how often it is that a bus or a group of buses left Banja Luka. So let me ask that question again. Just talking about the frequency, on a monthly average, how many - I'm going to call them convoys - how many convoys would leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On a monthly basis, it may have been twice, departures from Banja Luka, perhaps three departures. The nature of the activities was quite complex, but we can see about that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When these buses were leaving twice, maybe three times on a monthly basis, typically how many buses would leave as a group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On average, two or three. On average. Sometimes only one. Sometimes two. I do remember that once, however, once only, there were five or six buses leaving together. But this only happened once. As for the rest, there would be one, two, or three buses leaving at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In order to become a passenger on a bus, was there a procedure that needed to be followed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I heard, in order to become a passenger on a bus, there was a procedure to be followed. Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, was there a procedure that needed to be followed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the agency charge a fee for the bus service?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No -- yes, for transport. Yes, everyone needed to purchase a ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And could you purchase the ticket in dinars or Deutschmarks? What currency would the agency want?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly in dinars. Whichever citizens did not have dinars, they were free to pay in Deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you remember what the fee was the six months that you were the head of the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The travel fee was also regulated by the town's laws. It was the same fee that other regular bus lines applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where did the fee go once it was collected by representatives of the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The money would be paid by citizens into the account and bring pay slips. The agency had an account, and that's where the money was paid. The citizen would normally bring back a pay note or a pay slip proving that they purchased their ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm at a good stopping point, and it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. We'll stop here for a short break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin is here. Mr. Cunningham, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Before the break, we were at that point where I was going to have you discuss the procedure to be followed if one wanted to leave, so let's start there. If I was an individual who wanted to leave Banja Luka between July 1992 and the end of the year of 1992 and I came to your agency, how would it be that I got on a bus? Was there certain paperwork that I needed to supply to the agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would it work? Walk us through the process. I'm -- take a typical person who comes to the agency who wants to leave either for Gradiska or Vlasic. What's the first thing that they do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The procedure would be as follows: First you would approach the agency and tell them what your wishes and intentions are. You wish to travel. Then you get the instructions. You need to obtain a document that you have registered out of your place of residence. If you have obtained such a document, then you can be put on the list of persons scheduled for the travel. Unless you have obtained the document, you cannot be put on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When you talk about this document to show that you have registered out of your place of residence, how would one go about getting that document? Who do you go to to get that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This document can be obtained from any municipality, that is, from the municipality where the person concerned is residing. And that is with the Ministry of the Internal Affairs, that is, the police. They hold all the information concerning the persons residing in the area. If there are no problems involved, for instance, you are not under any criminal investigation or you have not been charged with anything, you can obtain the document there. You can be registered out of your place of residence there. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If I was travelling -- if an individual was travelling from Banja Luka going to a Western country, say, the Netherlands, Sweden, a place like that, was it ever necessary to have a letter of acceptance or a letter of guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The person travelling knows, of course, what his or her destination is and whether they can reach the destination. If they need a letter of guarantee from, for instance, Sweden or The Netherlands, then this person would be the one to ask the agency to try and obtain the letter of guarantee from their friends. In some cases, the letter of guarantee was not required; in others, it was. It all depended on the wishes of the person travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your answer, you said something I don't quite understand. You said: "This person would be the one to ask the agency to try and obtain a letter of guarantee from their friends." Would the agency actually be the one to contact the individual in The Netherlands or Sweden or whatever that Western country may be for that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Rather, the people in Sweden or The Netherlands would be sending such letters to the AR Krajina; that is, these letters would first arrive in Zagreb, and then would be forwarded to the border where the persons travelling would arrive. So our employees would be the ones to bring these letters of guarantees and deliver them to the persons to whom they were addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And again, there's something in your answer that confuses me, because you said that these letters of guarantee would first arrive in Zagreb, and then be forwarded to the border. Would they be forwarded to Zagreb, or be forwarded to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: To Banja Luka. But this was the way of actually having it arrive in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'm still not clear on it. One more time. How would it arrive in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The letter would reach the border, for instance, at Okucani or any other town controlled by the Croatian authorities. When the buses carrying passengers from Banja Luka would reach that particular location, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the -- our operative employees, Bandic and Segrt, would apply to the Croatian authorities asking whether there are any documents for Banja Luka citizens, any documents that arrived by mail. And then if there is -- if there was something, if there was a letter of guarantee, then the Croatian authorities would hand it over to us. If not, then nothing would come of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were those -- your employees authorised to do that, what you've just described, to pick up the letters and do the transfers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: They did have the authorisation. They were supposed to do so because this was one of the services provided by the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. So after an individual goes to the agency with the proper documentation, what's the next step? Is that when the individual's put on a list to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The person has to bring the document testifying to the fact that the person has registered out of its municipality of residence. And then the list of persons is made, and the list is then double-checked in Banja Luka. And once it has been established that the list is a final one, then the persons involved have to purchase their ticket and can travel by bus when scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the notebook, go to the exhibit marked 253, please. When you find that document, read it to yourself and let us know when you're done.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is this exhibit, DB253, an example of what you're just talking about, that is, that the persons involved purchasing their ticket and then travelling on the bus when scheduled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I look here at the top of that document, and it says: "In October 1992, the payment is 14.000 dinars." What was the purchasing power of 14.000 dinars --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was the purchasing power of that amount of money in October of 1992 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: You could have bought two kilogrammes of meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right. We've talked about how passengers get on the list. Let's now switch topics and talk about how the buses were acquired for the actual transportation. Who was -- was there any particular person within the agency that was responsible for locating and securing the buses for transport?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Bandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Was there -- were there negotiations over the price of the bus rental, or how was the fee set for the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The fee for the bus was not something arbitrarily determined by the agency. It was determined by the regulations governing regular passenger travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I failed to ask you this question earlier, but I take it that the agency did not have its own fleet of buses but had to hire buses or rent buses to take passengers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It did not have its own fleet of buses or its own vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After the list of passengers is set, after the buses have been hired, is there still a security concern that needs to be addressed before the buses can leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And tell the Chamber if you would, please, what steps were taken with respect to security.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: If there was need to ensure safer transportation for the passengers, we asked for the protection by the police. Otherwise, those travelling were escorted by our operative employees, Segrt and Bandic. Otherwise, passengers would be travelling regardless of the fact whether police escort was required or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would you determine if a police escort was required? What steps would be taken?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was a simple procedure. The operative employees escorting the bus, once they have done their job, they submit a report as to whether the trip was a safe one. And particularly at the line of separation between the two armies, if there were no war operations, the passengers could travel. If there are war operations, then the passengers cannot go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So I take it -- well, I don't want to lead. Were there ever instances that trips were cancelled because of security concerns caused by military operations near the roads that the passengers would travel on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever determine that it would be appropriate for a bus or a group of buses to leave, but with a police escort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: If the assistance of the police was required, then we always asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your notebook, please, find first of all the yellow tab marked 256, go to that, read it to yourself and let us know when you're done with it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is that document dated 13 November 1992 an example of your request for a police escort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Go to Exhibit 259, and I want you to find that tab with the number 259. Read it to yourself because I want to ask you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is that another example of what we just talked about a minute ago, that is, a request to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After the security arrangements had been made, the passenger lists compiled, the monies collected, what would be the next step?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The next step would be to establish the time of travel. Once this has been done, the passengers are notified of the time of travel. Usually the departures took place in the morning around 8.00, 9.00, or 10.00. The persons travelling would show up at the place that was previously agreed upon and at the scheduled time. And if there were two buses, then they would be numbered 1 or 2. And by these numbers, you could always know which passengers were supposed to go to bus 1 and which to bus 2. The persons were roll-called, and upon hearing their name they would take their seat on the bus. Because the passengers didn't have a ticket bearing the number of the seat, which wasn't really important. The important thing was that the passengers had their seats. They could take their seats. And once this was done, the departure took place to the desired destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go through and break down your answer in a little bit more detail. First of all, where would the buses typically depart from? Would they depart from the agency? Where would they leave from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Outside the agency. There was an area of some five --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: And the bus could fit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you present and could you observe what happened when the buses would leave from that location?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Not always. Sometimes. Our operative employees were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure. And what I want you to do is to talk about your personal knowledge, what you saw those times that you saw the buses leave. This location, first of all, that we've talked about, was that a public location or was it private?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Public location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would the location of the departure be posted to the public?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Would individuals who wanted to leave Banja Luka, would they be required to come alone, by themselves, or could they be accompanied by friends, family, relatives?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was up to them. They could have shown up alone or in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. company of their friends. It was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you observed buses leaving, did you see -- happen to see passengers saying their farewells to friends and family, or who would appear to be friends and family?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sometimes we know from looking, for example, at -- and you don't need to look at this, I'm just using it as an example -- from looking at Exhibit 259, this was two buses heading from Banja Luka towards Vlasic, and it's a request for security. Those instances where the security service centre was providing security, what would the officers, the police officers be doing as the passengers were arriving at the scene and then making ready for their departure on the buses? What would those officers do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. They would be in their vehicle, and they weren't interested in this procedure, in the employees doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The times that you observed buses leaving that had security like we've just described, did you personally ever see police officers maltreat, do anything improper with passengers getting on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: While you were present and watching these buses get loaded and passengers made ready to travel, did you ever see any civilians maltreat the people who were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever see the police ever attempt to extort, demand, take money or property from passengers as they were making ready to leave or boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did you ever see any civilian, and just as importantly, any of your operative employees, do the same? That is, extort, demand, take money or personal property from passengers that were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the agency ever try to limit the amount of money that a departing person could take with him or her?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The agency didn't have the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to show you -- I'd like to show you an exhibit. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit P227. This, for the record, is the ARK Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what I'd like to do, Mr. Usher, is if you can find -- I apologise for not having a B/C/S copy for this witness. But we need to find entry number 26. Entry number 26 is on page 44 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I'm going to read you what this decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, issued on 3 June 1992, approximately three and a half weeks before you started, says. Article 3 reads as follows: "Natural persons leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina may take out a maximum of 300 Deutschmarks or corresponding amounts in other currencies which may not exceed this limit. Amounts of foreign currency which persons refer to in paragraph 1 of this article may take out pursuant to Articles 8, 21, and 28 of the decree on official business travel expenses and establishment of residence abroad which for the organs and organisations of federal administration are recognised as material expenses shall be limited by present regulations. Amounts exceeding the limit prescribed in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article which the persons refer to in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article, attempt to take out, shall be confiscated." Did you as head of this agency ever receive any directives, any orders, any suggestions, anything whatsoever that told you to limit the amount of money departing passengers could take with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever ride along these routes with buses of passengers? I should say a busload of passengers.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how many times did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Once when we were headed for Vlasic, and once in the direction of Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about those two separate trips. Let's go ahead and take the trip to Gradiska. How is it -- why did you go along on that trip?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There were two reasons for this. Firstly, I wanted to experience in person what the ride was like, how the passengers felt on the trip. Secondly, I had at the time friends of mine, Muslims, on the bus. And as a person, I felt the need to escort them to the border and to part with them there. I did not want to wait in Banja Luka. On the bus, there was a wife and two daughters of a colleague of mine who worked with me in a secondary school. And that was this once.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you say the colleague with the wife and two daughters, was that colleague a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The day that you rode the bus with your colleague's wife and children, what was the nationality, if you know, of the people that were leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent certain. But there were different ethnicities there. Muslims, Croats, Slovenes, I believe, Serbs. I'm not sure if there was anyone else. But I am certain about those that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you made this trip to Gradiska, what was the procedure? Did it differ any from what I had you -- what you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was no different. Everything was the same as earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When you boarded the bus, how many people were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
