utterances.text: Everything was done in compliance with regulations. There was a regulation governing how many people you were allowed to fit on to a bus. The bus, for example, could have 52 seats, and then in practice a mother would have been allowed to have two children on two other seats. But not more -- no more people were allowed on to the buses than could be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And was that the practice and procedure of the agency, not only for this trip, but for other trips?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this was regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, this bus trip that you took to escort your family's -- your colleague's family, did the bus go all the way to Zagreb or did it stop short of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed back in Gradiska, but the bus drove on. As far as the Croat-controlled line. I don't think the bus drove on after that, past the Croat-controlled line. I don't think it did; that was the established practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And from Gradiska across the Sava to the Croat-controlled line, do you know how long that would be? What distance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As you rode the bus from Banja Luka to Gradiska, were you accompanied by a police escort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was the bus that you were travelling with with your Muslim colleague's family, was it ever stopped by men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time that you were with the bus and escorting your colleague's family, was there -- did you see anyone on that bus being maltreated?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did your colleague's wife and family arrive safely at their ultimate destination?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They called me from Paris ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was their attitude? How did they react to their safe arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to travel through Travnik. There was fighting between Croats and Muslims going on down there, so the agency did not approve the route on account of the safety of those travelling. Once they had passed the Croatian border and reached Zagreb, a friend of mine, Meho Sihalic [phoen], a geography teacher called to thank me for the fact that his family had arrived safely. His children were very young. I used to be Santa Claus for his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I had to say this. You almost have the right hair colour for it. I guess I really don't have any room to joke --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You also told us you made the trip to Travnik. How many times did you make the trip actually not to Travnik but to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How many times did you make that trip?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was your reason for making this trip?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: To assure myself personally of what the journey itself looked like, how safe it was, and just to be there with the people travelling because they placed great confidence in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When -- obviously you were there as the passengers were boarding the bus. Did you observe anything improper going on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the -- were the buses boarded like you've described earlier, in the same location at roughly the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything went fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through it step by step. The nationalities, the ethnicity of the people that were on the bus, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. As they were -- as -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. There were people from mixed marriages, too, here and there, the occasional mixed marriage between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Whoever felt that it was safer for them to go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Was this -- how many buses were in this group of buses that were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: One. One.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was it escorted by anyone from the Security Services Centre or any other police or law enforcement agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, there were Bandic and Segrt on behalf of the agency, the usual escort. The public security station provided two police officers driving an official vehicle following the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did those police officers either at the point of departure or anywhere along the route ever do anything improper? By that I mean attempt to get any money, personal property, jewellery, or anything like that from any person on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was the bus ever stopped along its route and boarded by anyone who treated passengers improperly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there anything improper or unusual or illegal as that bus made its way from Banja Luka towards Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The road across the mountain is not of the same quality as roads in the town. Aside from that, everything was as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What about the seating arrangements? Was this -- you told us earlier that there were regulations that limited the amount of passengers that could ride in a bus. Was that regulation observed on this trip?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There may have been four or five passengers more than could be seated. But this was something you couldn't sort out on the spot because those were families after all. You couldn't leave someone behind in Banja Luka and take all the others away. Regulations were complied with, but on this particular occasion, I think there were four or five people more on the bus than the bus could actually seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Where was the drop-off point, if you will, for passengers on the buses travelling from Banja Luka to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The place is called Galica. It's a mountain pass where passengers would get off the bus. And at that point, there was a kilometre or two left for them to walk before they reached Muslim-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Were you satisfied with -- well, what was your reaction as the chief of that agency after you had made the trip from Banja Luka to Galica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Every smooth journey, whenever there was a smooth journey, and there were never any problems, I was extremely satisfied because I knew that all the those people were only leaving temporarily. I knew they would be back sometime later, and that I would see all of them again. I shared their grief. I shared their vicissitudes, and I encouraged people. The hardest thing for me was to watch children travelling because there was no way for me to explain to them what the whole thing was about. I was happy to be in a position to provide my services, whatever services I was in a position to provide to people. But that's what I do after all. I teach. I teach young people to uphold standards of humanity, to show character, to be honest, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me -- I'm going to talk to you about your salaries, because in evidence as both Prosecution and Defence exhibits are the payrolls first from July of 1992, then from December of 1992. Let's just first of all go to Exhibit 290. That would be number 2-9-0 on the yellow tab in your binder. This is the payroll documents for July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please give me the number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir. 2-9-0.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: First of all, it says "payment in dinars," "payment in Deutschmarks". What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Only in dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how was -- for example, we see the third column over, it says: "Coefficient." How was it that your salary was determined? What does that coefficient have to do with your salary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The coefficient is the equivalent of your education level. People who have merely completed secondary school cannot have the same salary as people who have a university education. So that's what the coefficient means. Secondly, the level of complexity entailed in someone's work varies from individual to individual, which again affects their salaries. The coefficient is official. This is something that is determined under law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. We look at Exhibit 290, it shows that your net amount is what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: 16.900 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want you to look at, if you please, Exhibit 277, which is the payroll records for December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It looks like the fourth column in, it shows your net amount. And what is that net amount?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Based on this document, my amount was 93.381 dinars. The other people on the list had the salaries indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, if we were to compare July's payroll with December's payroll, it almost looks like you had a raise of -- a fivefold raise; that is, you went from approximately 17.000 to approximately 94.000 dinars. Did you, in fact, get such a raise?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: This strikes me as a bit strange. This is actually a decrease in salaries on account of the inflation rate. Every ten days, the dinar would drop, plummet, in relation to the mark. So this amount of money, it seems like there has been an increase, but it's not actually true. As for the exchange rate between the dinar and the German mark, it was published every day in the Glas daily paper. It was no secret really.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What would be the purchasing power in December 1992 or January 1993 when you got paid for approximately 94.000 dinars? What could you buy with that sort of money?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite say right now, but it was a very small salary, insufficient to cover all the needs of an average person through a month. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Not a single member of a family, let alone families with two, three, four or more persons. I couldn't say exactly what you could buy with this kind of money, but it would not have been sufficient to cover even a third of average monthly expenditure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you married, or are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was married, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The amount of money that you received in January 1993, approximately 94.000 dinars, was that enough for you to support yourself, your wife, and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to a different exhibit, and that exhibit is marked 278. I want you to find that document and read it to yourself. And once you are done with it, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This was also exhibited as P1689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I want to mention that all these three exhibits which were previously exhibited by the Prosecution were exhibited under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, I wish I would have known that earlier, Your Honour, because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit DB278, this is an authorisation. What is this authorisation all about? What purpose did this document do -- serve, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of this document is to authorise persons to talk to representatives of the Croatian authorities on behalf of the agency and discuss possible cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Early this morning -- earlier this morning, we talked about Prosecutor's Exhibit 241, and we don't need to exhibit it, that's the decision of 12 June 1992 appointing you to the chief of the agency. Did you ever have any contact with Mr. Brdjanin, any of his representatives, after you took control of this agency?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, the asked-and-answered objection. He has already answered that one. If you want to ask him again, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He just answered it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, how would you respond to people who criticised you and your agency as people who were in effect stealing from the non-Serb population who were trying to get out of Banja Luka? Is that a valid criticism?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I have never heard any such criticism uttered while I was working. First I hear of it. It strikes me as illogical. If there are persons who address the agency, why would they need to address the agency in the first place if they knew that the agency was stealing from them, robbing them, and taking them somewhere they wouldn't necessarily be safe? There's no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. logic in this. It just wouldn't have worked had the agency really been involved in robbery, in stealing, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, how do you -- you've talked about logic. I want to hear your personal reaction. If someone were to criticise you and your agency that in 1992, that you were stealing from people who were desperate to leave Banja Luka, would that be a valid criticism? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. This didn't happen. This would not have been possible. There were people living in Banja Luka, citizens facing great difficulty. Refugees coming from the area of the Federation, coming from Croatia. Those people would not have allowed such things to happen. They would not have allowed some people to steal, to make profit, while other people were on the front facing great danger to their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did your tenure, the time you spent with the agency, go to satisfy your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure. Did the time that you spent with the agency, did that excuse you -- well, obviously did, because you've testified from it. Forget that last question because I think you can answer it better by answering this question: When you -- when your job ended in -- at the end of December 1992, what happened to you? Did you go back to teaching?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I went back to teaching, which is what I actually do professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And how soon were you back in the teaching profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 15th of March 1993. Therefore, you see, in the meantime, there were half-term holidays, so I started working in the second term, on the 15th of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Ms. Korner, do you want to start -- I'm sorry. Madam Richterova, do you want to start straight away, or do you want to have the break now and start later?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, we can start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, let's suspend the sitting for one minute, two minutes. --- Break taken at 12.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies to you, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I did not get a copy of the exhibits the OTP plans to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure that was an oversight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, it's not an oversight. The fact is we don't actually know what these witnesses are going to say until they say it. So there's only a provisional list that is prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was an oversight certainly not handing it to Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were given now the provisional list, Your Honour. It could have been given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's only handed out once the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Yes, you are going to be cross-examined by the Prosecution now, Madam Richterova will be putting the questions to you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bojinovic. I will start with --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- with the part you were talking about your first meeting with Mr. Brdjanin which took place sometime in 1991. And you said: "I spoke about the need for every intellectual to have common sense, to try to be active in their own environment, to try to explain to those who are less knowledgeable, to try to tell them to remain calm, to not provoke incidents." When you were talking about these intellectuals and about these less knowledgeable, did you -- or do you consider to be an intellectual?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It is for the others to say if I am or am not. In the area I come from, everyone who has graduated from a university is considered to be a sort of an intellectual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were a teacher. And if I understood correctly, you were not a head teacher; you were just an ordinary teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a headmaster. I was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which means you had no managerial experience either in 1990, 1991, or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you stated that when you were appointed the director of this agency, you didn't receive any instruction, you weren't told what to do, how to do it. Do you consider it right that you, as an intellectual --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you as an intellectual, intelligent person, you took a job about which you didn't know absolutely anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was a proper thing to do because these duties were of later date. Something that was not known before came up as a result of the circumstances. Probably those who took this decision of who to appoint as head of the agency, they probably wanted to have an intellectual, a person who had good communicative skills, who had a psychological insight into the people and could be of help under the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will talk about your work with the agency at some later stage. Now, I would like to ask you about your membership in the SDS. When did you -- when did you become a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Officially in 1991. And unofficially as soon as the SDS had been established, I was a follower of this party. I adhered to its programme just as my people did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why do you say "unofficially"? What do you mean by stating "unofficially"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: First, a party has to be established in order to have members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you participate at these initial steps of setting up of the party together with Jovan Raskovic or Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you participate in all the meetings which took place in Drvar during the year 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You didn't participate in any, or did you participate in some of these?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Drvar on the 4th of July as a common citizen. I didn't know either of the two men. And in Sarajevo on the 12th of July in 1990, I was there with all the other citizens. I was even in contact with the late Izetbegovic. And that's about it as concerns my acquaintances. I wasn't an organiser. I was just an anonymous person, and my community is also a very small one, and I could not have really been an organiser or an ideologist of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: A second ago you said: "I was a follower of this party. I adhered to its programme just as my people did." Who are "my people"? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serbian people because up to then, you only had one party in the former Yugoslavia. It was the League of Communists. And I never really agreed with the League of Communists' programme. When Yugoslavia came to be dissolved, then the peoples living in the area -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. We know about the League of Communists. I was just -- if you could answer just my question. And if I need some more information, I would ask you. You mentioned you were in Drvar on 4th of July 1990. Were you ever a member of -- and I'm talking about these initial steps or initial meetings. Were you ever a member or candidate for the position of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. member of the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1990 following the establishment of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you were a member of the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object for the form of the question because he said he wasn't a member of the main board. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, what he said yes was to "were you ever a member or a candidate for the position of member of the member of the main board of the SDS," so I think my objection is valid because it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Were you a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. So you were only a candidate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you were a candidate to become a member of the main board. So it means that you belong among the organisers of the party or the policy of this party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened -- you said you were on the candidate list. Were you appointed a member --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you appointed a member of the main board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you politically active in your municipality, in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Milorad Bojinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was it? Who was him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: He was the gentleman who passed away a couple of months ago. He lived in Banja Luka, if this is the person you are talking about, who worked in the pension/disability insurance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I was talking about one Milorad Bojinovic from Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is him. He moved over to Banja Luka and lived there. If you are talking about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this Milorad Bojinovic the president of the SDS in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the name -- what was the name of the first president of the SDS in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the establishment of the SDS, there was no president. And after the SDS was established in 1990, I think it was Milorad Babic. Babic. That's his family name. But I'm not sure about his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And for how long was this Milorad Babic president of the SDS in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was still president during the war, but many people changed, were replaced during the war, and I wasn't really keeping contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you stated that you were candidate for the main board of the SDS, you followed the policy. Can you tell us why you weren't politically active in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was never really attracted by politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So why was this reason that right from 1990 you were involved in the setting up of the party, of the party of your people, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has understood your question. It's certainly not your fault, Madam Richterova. I will -- with your indulgence, I will put the question again myself. You've just told us, Mr. Bojinovic, that you were never really interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is so, how come that you involved yourself in precisely the setting up of a political party, namely, the SDS, if you were not interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The setting up of a political party is something that came out of the circumstances in 1990. I was interested in the fate, not only of my people, but of the entire area of the former Yugoslavia, which doesn't mean that I had any political pretensions. From the party's establishment to this date, I have never held any political duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And only one more question, I again, repeat this, that you were a candidate for the main board of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, which is quite an important position. So you say "I was not interested in politics," so what was the reason that you stand for this rather important position in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably the people appreciated me, the people in my community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just because the people appreciated you as a person, it was the reason why you stand for this -- for this important position within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any other reasons. But I think this was the main one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it was the people who wanted you to be a member, but it was not you who wanted to be a member of the main board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to the meeting which occurred in Banja Luka in 1991 during which you met Mr. Brdjanin. You were introduced to Mr. Brdjanin by one Ljupko Racic, if this is correct. Who was this man, Ljupko Racic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him from before. He wrote poetry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you met him by chance in Banja Luka, or did he accompany you to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. He lived in Banja Luka, and I knew him as a poet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was it him who took you to the Hotel Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Rather, he had told me that one could have a drink at Hotel Bosna, that he went there quite frequently, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you went to Hotel Bosna with Mr. Ljupko Racic, and how did you meet Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There were people seated around a table, as is usual. And also as usual, then you get to know these people, people introduce themselves. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Ljupko Racic who introduced you to Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I merely came up and shook hands with everyone. It wasn't really a formal introduction by this gentleman we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us who else apart from Mr. Brdjanin was that day in the Hotel Bosna sitting around the same table with you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know other people from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And why do you remember that Mr. Brdjanin was there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin was well known as a sportsman, and it is only natural that when I got to know that the person in front of me was him, I knew him because he had been known to show up in the mass media as a sportsman. But I had not met him personally earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was he introduced only as a sportsman, or was he also introduced in his professional capacity or any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: As a sportsman, because I am keen on sports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you were introduced as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. As Milos Bojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you talk about your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: At this particular meeting we did not talk about our occupations. It was just an ordinary chat over a drink as happens in similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You testified that you talk about politics during this meeting. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Whether you can term it as politics or not, but we talked about the emerging situation which wasn't particularly nice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I will read you what you stated. "We discussed politics because the situation in the area was complex. The discussion was just an ordinary one. No particular plans were being hatched as to what could happen." Why were you talking about plans? Were there any plans at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know of. I have no knowledge of any plans. At this particular meeting, there were people who happened to be there by chance, and of course they didn't go there to discuss anything specific. We merely talked of a situation which was complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And why did you mention in your testimony, why did you mention this plan? Why did you mention the word "plan"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, another term could have been used instead of "plan," but the question was what did you talk about and whether there were any plans. Well, there were no plans. I am not an engineer, nor a high-ranked politician planning anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I didn't -- it wasn't me who was talking about plans; it was you who said, and I quote: "No particular plans were being hatched as to what could happen." You said it. So why did you say it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could explain it the following way: Normally people talk about the goings on, the plans that are in existence and so on. My logical answer to that is there were no plans -- or instead of saying plans, you could say there were no specific arrangements. This term "plan" could be replaced by a number of alternatives. So it might be an important thing to you as a Tribunal, "plan"; to me, it is just an ordinary word.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that for the time being. Mr. Bojinovic, we are going to have another break for 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you will finish today, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would appreciate then if you could leave us just a few minutes, or rather you can take up to the very end, because I only need one or two minutes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to actually ask if we could have a few minutes at the end anyhow because I want to try and sort out the witnesses again. So perhaps if Ms. Richterova could stop at around half past 1.00, because we'll certainly finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's perfect. That would suit us perfectly well. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, before the break we were talking about the meeting which you had with people in Hotel Bosna among which Mr. Brdjanin was present. And we were talking about this word "plan." And I again will quote what you said: "Normally people talk about the goings on, the plans that are in existence, about specific arrangements. There were no such plans." My question is "no such plans," plans for what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what plans people could be hatching who only just met for the very first time. There were no plans. We just chatted away over a drink. This word "plan," I'm not sure what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As I said, it was you who mentioned this word. And it is the reason why I am asking you. But you were just talking. Can you be a little bit more specific and very briefly tell us what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: We just met by chance. Everyone wanted to say something just by way of introduction. I can only tell you what I was talking about. But after so many years, you can hardly expect me to remember what the other people were saying. I can hardly remember what I had for lunch yesterday, let alone what people were saying at a completely meaningless meeting ten years ago. I can tell you what I said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you would be repeating. You have already told us what you said, unless you have anything different or anything new to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- he said that they were talking about politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, and he said before that the situation was such that one needed to stay calm. It's -- if there's anything else, let's hear, but I think it's a series of questions and answers that are not going to lead us anywhere. So the message, according to what I understood, was that the discussion was very general, generic, not specific. That's what I understood. I'm not going to stop you, Ms. Richterova. Don't misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will ask you this: You mentioned this meeting was sometime in the year 1991. Can you recollect approximately in which part of that year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can with any degree of precision whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it after the war in Croatia started?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when the war started in Croatia. I don't know when. Therefore, I'm not able to tell you anything about that, not with certainty at any rate. I know that the war in Croatia began in 1991, but I couldn't give you the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were -- you mentioned that you were talking about your opinions. Were you talking about the policy of the SDS? And if I presume, you were all members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if any of the people there were members, in fact. I know that I myself was a member. If any of the others were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin mention that he was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he mention which position he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he worked at the time in Banja Luka or in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have any private conversation with Mr. Brdjanin at that time or at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it the only time -- until the moment you were appointed the director of the agency, was it the only time you met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at that time you met him in 1991, you didn't mention that you were a teacher, he didn't mention what position he held. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. But I don't think it would have been necessary for anyone to say what their profession was. This is usually referred to as boasting where I come from. I didn't find out about the professions of any of the people present back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you didn't exchange addresses, telephones, anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And very last question, during -- about this meeting is I just -- you said you do not remember who else was present. I will just tell you randomly some names, and you can tell us whether you remember by any chance that such a person would be present. Vojo Kupresanin, was he present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him being there. I was not exactly in touch with him. I don't think he was there, but I can't be sure. I'm not sure of any of the people because that was the first time we met. I'm only sure about Mr. Brdjanin being there. I did not know any of the other people at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And Radislav Vukic? Was he present?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the name for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Radislav Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Vukic. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you are so sure that Mr. Brdjanin was present at that meeting? You say there were ten people. You do not remember anybody else but Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. There were about ten people there. I'm not sure if it was ten, nine, eight. Mr. Brdjanin has a very striking appearance physically. He's an athlete. He's the kind of person you tend to remember. What you don't remember doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, Mr. Brdjanin became a politician, a public figure. Did you follow his career after this meeting when you were able to say I met such a sportsman, such an important person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really have anyone else's careers in mind. It wasn't my business. It was their own business. I didn't really follow Mr. Brdjanin's career or anyone else's.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But what I am saying, I understand that it's everybody's business which career he or she follows. But he became a public figure. You met him. You became an acquaintance of him based on this meeting. So did you follow his professional development?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I object. That's repetitive. It has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but -- it is repetitive in a way, Mr. Cunningham. I'm going to allow the question because the witness did not exactly answer the previous question that was put to him. He answered it partially and at a tangent. So please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please repeat the question in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I can repeat the question. My question was: Mr. Brdjanin became a public figure. Did you -- and you met him. You became an acquaintance of his. Did you follow his professional development after the meeting, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean by "follow." You mean watch whenever he appeared on TV, read about him in the printed media, or whether I had a personal insight into his activities. Can you please specify.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I can elaborate. I mean, were you able to attend any rallies in which he would be present? Or did you read any interviews with him in any kind of newspaper articles? Did you watch him, did you see him on television?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I never attended any rallies whatsoever. As for Mr. Brdjanin as someone who was very much in the public eye, it was there for all to read in the papers. You could see it on TV whenever they showed anything like that. Anyone could see it. Anyone who was able to read or switch on a TV set.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I am not talking about anyone; I am talking about you. And my question is whether you followed his development, whether you were able to say, "this is Mr. Brdjanin," and he is whatever he was at the time you watched the TV, you read the newspaper article about him.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you read -- you knew what was his position? You were able to learn his position from what you read in the newspaper? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what you see on television or what you learned from any other sources. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid the question is not clear. Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think I will move on. You answered it -- my previous question. I want to ask, were you aware that Mr. Brdjanin became a vice-president of the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That he became president of the ARK Crisis Staff? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So because you said that you were able to follow Mr. Brdjanin, or better say, his professional development, what did you learn about him? What was he? Was he just a sportsman, and you read about Mr. Brdjanin as a sportsman? Or what did you read about Mr. Brdjanin or what did you see on television about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to object, but there's six different questions there, and I'd ask as best as she could to limit her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- to avoid the compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ackerman -- Mr. Cunningham. Mr. Cunningham understands why I keep saying Mr. Ackerman. Let's split this question into parts, Madam Richterova, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just stated that you didn't know that Mr. Brdjanin was vice-president of the ARK, that he was the president of the crisis staff. Did you know that he was a politician?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you know from what you read in a newspaper that Mr. Brdjanin was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was a minister for construction. But that was only later. That was after the ARK. You're talking to me -- you're asking me about his position as vice-president of the Krajina Assembly. But at that point, I knew nothing about that, and I knew nothing about that before Mr. Brdjanin became the minister for construction and civil engineering. I think that's what it's called. It was only after that you could read about him in the papers, about ministers, about government members. It was the daily kind of thing that was in the press.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, do you want to tell the Judges that you never read or heard anything about Mr. Brdjanin during the year of 1991 and the first half of the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: It simply wasn't possible. I was in Glamoc at the time, which is a very small town. And it's far away from Banja Luka. We did not get any press, daily press from Banja Luka. We had the general Bosnia and Herzegovina press. We only had the daily, Oslobodjenje, which as a rule contained no information whatsoever on Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were not allowed -- you were not able to read the Glas newspaper in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you were not able to receive Banja Luka TV in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no such thing as Banja Luka TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At a later stage when there was Banja Luka TV? Did you watch it either in Glamoc or in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to be accurate. I arrived in Banja Luka on the 1st of July 1992. Prior to that, I had no information from TV or the press on Mr. Brdjanin. He was not a person in the public eye before that time, before I arrived in Banja Luka. He came into the public eye, at least as far as I was aware, after he had been appointed minister. But this was already 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you mentioned that you were mobilised approximately in April 1992. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At that time, you were a teacher. You were 40 -- approximately 45 year old. Was it normal that an intellectual, a teacher, would be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And he would be mobilised and sent to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also told us that you learned about your appointment to the position of director of this agency while you were in the -- on the front line. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you were informed verbally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who conveyed this message to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: The messenger of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the message? Was it you got a position, or was it already specific what kind of position you were going to hold?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was nothing specific. According to the rules of service that applied in the army, the messenger would inform any soldier to report to the command. That was the procedure followed. Let me add this, too. The command informed me that I had been informed and advised of my duty to report to Banja Luka following my appointment to one of the agencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this happened when? Do you remember how many days before you left for Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: That was a day or two before I arrived in Banja Luka. This happened at the same time as my regular leave that every soldier is entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you report to your commander. And were you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So how it was possible that you left the army, that you left the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were mobilised, you were in the army, you were at the front line. You received the message to report in Banja Luka. You left for Banja Luka, but you say that you were not demobilised. How is that possible that you started working? Were you still mobilised at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and explain. I left for Banja Luka. I was told about my duties. My duty was to go back to my command to complete my military stint with that particular unit. Once I'd done that, I was as a consequence demobilised, which means that I ceased to be a soldier with the unit that I had originally come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were supposed to go to Banja Luka. Where were you -- where did you report yourself in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: I reported to Mr. Blagojevic. We have referred to him today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was it a part of this message that you were supposed to contact Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: There was no special recommendation, if that's what you have in mind. The decision on my assignment stated clearly in the heading "the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And then I asked, who is the man in charge? Who is the man I should report to? I talked to people on the street, and I asked them the question. And they told me such and such a man is occupying such and such a position, that is the building. And that's how I found him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, but you stated that you received the information about your appointment verbally first. And second, in fact, you didn't know what kind of --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- Assignment you received.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So how did you know that you were supposed to contact Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was informed that this had come straight from the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I asked around who was there, who was in charge of these affairs. And then people on the street told me where the offices of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were, and I went there. I spoke to staff as soon as I got there. I didn't know who they were. They said: "Go and speak to Mr. Blagojevic," and that's how I eventually reached him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be the right moment because I would like to discuss the appointment and the work of the agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Richterova. So Mr. Bojinovic, we are going to stop here today. We will continue tomorrow, and we hope to finish tomorrow so you can go back to your family. The usher will be escorting you out of this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour wanted to -- I know Your Honour said there was a matter you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the matter is I want to know roughly when to expect Mr. Ackerman back, because he's on my mind, of course. I want to clear a few things about the expected day of completion of the Defence case. And I don't want to burden you with all the responsibility, Mr. Cunningham, unless you are in a position to assume responsibility for some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm not ready to assume -- put that yoke on just quite yet. Mr. Ackerman can be here in the morning, I'm sure that wouldn't be a problem, or at a time that's convenient for this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason I'm saying this is because throughout Mr. Ackerman had been assuring us that he would be in a position to conclude the Defence case by the end of January, and now we're talking of the end of February or beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I know he's in a much better position to tell you where we stand. The other day I alluded to some of the concerns that potential witnesses were raising. And apparently, that's reared its ugly head more than one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And another thing I want to mention, I want to make sure that you are aware that we are sitting in the -- in January in the week starting on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right. We're aware of that and everything has been adjusted because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's also a concern that I had. I had a vague, vague -- obviously now I was wrong. I realise I was wrong. A vague impression that you were assuming that we were restarting on the 17th or 19th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I wish that was the case, but I have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's running along the same linings in a sense. As I recall, Mr. Ackerman, he said this visit to Banja Luka might shorten matters for the end of the January. And I fully appreciate, and it became absolutely clear to us that there was no conceivable way given there are only about another ten sitting days left of this year, and we don't start until the 12th of January. But Your Honour, what I'm concerned about is this, and I'll raise it for Mr. Ackerman to deal with tomorrow morning. First of all, I understand the problem. The third witness listed for next week, I gather, is not inclined or has reasons why he want turn up and will be rescheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Therefore, we would like to know obviously as soon as possible, if possible tomorrow, who the third witness next week is likely to be because the name of a witness was mentioned by Mr. Cunningham who isn't on any lists that we've got as intending to come before Christmas. Again, I say -- I'm not objecting to it, we would just like to know who's coming. We don't have any witnesses listed for after the week of the 8th of December. The only list we have been given by Mr. Ackerman is up until that week. And there's one more week sitting after that. So that's the next matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me try to address these concerns as quickly as I can. Witness number 38 has some concerns, and he is going to be rescheduled. What we were doing is trying to find a witness who would be of a similar length, and originally Witness number 42 came to mind. Witness Number 42 is hesitant for the reasons we've talked about before. We should know something about him this afternoon, whether he's coming or not. If he's not coming, what we -- what we're going to talk about doing is maybe moving up two of the one-day witnesses. I don't know which ones those will be. I hope to address the Court on that tomorrow. With respect to the week after that, because you had a concern over that, it is still our intention the week that I believe begins -- it's either 7 December or 8 December --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: 8 December, to start out with witness Number 34 and follow him up with Witness Number 40. Now, the people that we intended to follow that witness, they're up in the air because we're -- we don't know whether they're going to be moved up to next week or not. Ms. Korner, if helps you somewhat, at least it appears to me Witness Number 34, Witness Number 40 are -- I'd like to call them firm for the week of December 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, again it's the week after that. As Your Honour appreciates, as I've said over and over again, we have to prioritise the work that's done because there's many competing claims on the particular... Your Honour, the last matter is this, and I did send Mr. Cunningham an email yesterday, but for some reason he and I, our emails don't always communicate very well. I don't think he's received it. Can I just mention it. I also said I want to deal with that tomorrow, and that is I have listed what I described as the witnesses whose cross-examination is likely to be lengthy and asked for confirmation now that the visit to Banja Luka has taken place as to which, if not all of these witnesses will actually be attending. Because that obviously will effect the structure because as I said to Your Honours yesterday, we're going to make it very clear that we'll be asking for the witnesses to be in such a position to give sufficient time to properly cross-examine. So Your Honour, I've listed those, I don't think I need to go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I would prefer you didn't actually for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've only listed the ones as far as we know who as far as we know will testify in open session and just given numbers for the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. But I suppose that if the list or the information is communicated to Mr. Ackerman, he should be in a position to, if not confirm to us, at least liaise with the Prosecution on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I will bring that up with him this afternoon. And if I can communicate by way of email with Ms. Korner, I'll update her as best as I can electronically. Otherwise, Mr. Ackerman will be here in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, finally, and again Mr. Ackerman may want to deal with this, we have been told that we can't get any expert reports before Christmas. But also it appears there has been a change in the constitutional expert who I understood to be some lady from Belgrade or somewhere. But it appears it may be somebody different now. If it is somebody different, if we could be told tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Point taken. Anything else? My exhortation, if I may use that word, is to try and put us in a picture, the best picture possible, because we need as you can imagine with a case of this dimension, we need considerable time for our deliberations. And to liaise with the staff and meet amongst ourselves, meet amongst -- with our staff, draft parts ourselves, have other parts drafted for us. It's going to be a mammoth exercise. And every day that we can gain, you realise that we would be always in a better position. So expect us to do our best to gain as much time as we can. Okay? So we'll -- what I suggest, Madam Chuqing, can you copy this part for me, this part of the transcript after Madam Richterova finished so that I make notes of every point raised so that I'll make sure that everything is addressed tomorrow morning when hopefully Mr. Ackerman will be with us. All right. And please, we try and make sure that the witness will be in a position to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Definitely he will. He will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
